lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Imagine opening a browser tab and playing a classic NES or Super Nintendo game, from a server you run yourself. That's RetroArch Web Games.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the whole arcade, hosted at home?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Pretty much. Antoine packaged RetroArch, the emulator frontend, running in the browser, together with games for NES, SNES, Genesis and Game Boy in a single Docker image. You start it with docker compose up, and you've got a self-hosted web player.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And the games come with it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, pre-loaded. Scripts inside the image do the legwork: a bash function and a Python script download the game archives from several sources, then bash and Python rename the files and sort them into folders so RetroArch can list them cleanly. Downloads run in parallel with threads, and failures are reported instead of passing silently. It's like a librarian who fetches the books and shelves them for you.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Where does the image come from?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It builds on the retroarch-web work from Inglebard's Dockerfiles and the Emscripten package from the RetroArch project. It's published on Docker Hub under the MIT license.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: FlashGames, a small collection of legacy Flash games preserved for modern browsers with Ruffle.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Browser-based retro gaming, in one command. The project page has the details and the links.
